findings.stat_label: deposited item return vs peer median
findings.headline: One fee is an extreme outlier on an otherwise low-fee schedule.
findings.body: Your $40.00 deposited-item return fee is a flagged extreme outlier — 2.7x the $15 median of 27 peer banks, at the 100th percentile and tied for the highest in the cohort. It lands on customers whose deposited check bounced through no fault of their own, and it sits alone at the top of a schedule that is otherwise priced well below market.

findings.stat_label: your NSF fee vs peer median
findings.headline: You eliminated NSF fees — and nobody is hearing about it.
findings.body: You charge $0 for NSF against a $12 median across 35 peers, and $0 for card replacement against a $10 median. Eliminating the industry's most criticized fee is exactly the move regulators and consumer advocates have pushed for — a claim most of your cohort cannot make, and one your competitors' own published schedules substantiate. Today it earns you no visible credit.

findings.headline: Your money-movement fees are among the lowest in the cohort.
findings.body: International wires cost $10 against a $35 median (10th percentile), outgoing domestic wires $5 against a $20 median (13th percentile), and stop payments $15 against a $30 median (20th percentile). This is either a deliberate low-fee strategy that deserves marketing, or unclaimed margin across three categories — today it is priced like the former and promoted like neither.

exec_narrative: Net position: Hanmi Bank runs one of the most customer-friendly published fee schedules in its cohort — NSF and card-replacement fees eliminated outright, wire fees at the bottom decile, stop payments half the market. The glaring exception is a $40 deposited-item return fee, a flagged extreme outlier at 2.7x the peer median and the highest in a 27-bank cohort. That single line undercuts an otherwise coherent low-fee story. The agenda: decide whether the outlier survives, and decide whether the low-fee posture becomes a marketing asset instead of an accident of the price list.

callouts.title: Deposited item return — $40.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $15.00 · P75 $20.00 · 100th percentile · n=27 · flagged: extreme outlier (>2x median)
callouts.body: The customer being charged did nothing wrong — someone else's check failed. At $40 you charge more than any peer in the cohort and 2.7x the median, on a schedule where nearly everything else is below market. This is the one line a fee survey or examiner conversation will fix on; a cut toward the $15 median would make the schedule's low-fee story internally consistent.

callouts.title: NSF eliminated, card replacement free — the story is unmarketed
callouts.stat: NSF $0 vs $12 median (P6, waived, n=35) · Card replacement $0 vs $10 median (P11, waived, n=18)
callouts.body: Most cohort peers still charge both fees. 'We charge no NSF fee' is a concrete, verifiable differentiator on the exact line item that draws the most regulatory and press attention — and it is sitting unadvertised on your schedule. This belongs in acquisition marketing and branch messaging, substantiated by competitors' own published prices.

callouts.title: Wires and stop payments — bottom quintile of the cohort
callouts.stat: Intl wire $10 vs $35 median (P10) · Domestic outgoing $5 vs $20 median (P13) · Stop payment $15 vs $30 median (P20)
callouts.body: Three service categories priced at a fraction of the market. If deliberate, they reinforce the same low-fee positioning as the waived NSF fee and should be marketed with it. If not deliberate, note the headroom: even doubling these fees would leave each at or below its peer median.

callouts.title: Three categories unpublished — the comparison is incomplete
callouts.stat: No published data: ATM non-network · monthly maintenance · OD protection transfer
callouts.body: For an institution whose published fees are a competitive asset, gaps in the schedule work against you: comparison tools fill missing lines with assumptions, and customers cannot credit prices they cannot see. Publishing these three categories completes a schedule that, on the evidence, compares favorably almost everywhere.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: large banks have largely eliminated returned-item fees under regulatory and reputational pressure, and the trend is migrating through community cohorts — where your $0 NSF fee already puts you ahead of a market whose median still sits at $12. Second, deposit competition has turned fee schedules into marketing documents: published fees are public, scraped, and compared, which converts every below-market line into a provable claim and every outlier into a conspicuous exception.

Community-scale institutions ($1B–$10B) occupy the exposed middle: large enough to be included in comparisons, without the brand gravity that lets money-center banks charge premiums quietly. Your schedule is unusually well positioned for that exposure — provided the story is told and the one extreme outlier is resolved. The highest-leverage moves here are not cuts across the board; they are retiring or repricing a single $40 line item and converting an already-low fee schedule from a quiet fact into an active acquisition message.
